scenario: Today's retrieval track has three threads. The first is whether multi-hop and multimodal retrieval needs a graph built in advance. EAGR stores links between passages as metadata in a vector database, TrioRAG skips the graph and retrieves with three signals, and SkinMind turns a dermatology knowledge graph into tools that the model probes step by step. The second is what retrieval should keep, where FondueQA finds that a bridge document can be more useful than the one holding the answer. The third is base models and evaluation: SPARSEUP shows how to train sparse retrievers stably on new backbones, and two more papers build dedicated features and benchmarks for Vietnamese statutory retrieval and for hiring search.

papers.title: SPARSEUP: Towards Better Recipes for Training Modern Learned Sparse Retrievers
papers.authors: Thibault Formal, Pierre Erbacher, Cosimo Rulli
papers.abstract:
Learned sparse embeddings are a powerful alternative to dense retrieval, yet they have fallen behind single-vector and late interaction models. One reason for their limited adoption is that they are notoriously difficult to train, generally requiring very tight conditions to converge. We present a recipe for training Splade-like encoders on modern backbones and data that achieves a better efficiency-effectiveness trade-off.
We discuss the role of logit distribution and its impact on the training stability and the final sparsity of the encoder. We also introduce a new per-position fan-out control - a hard cap on how many vocabulary dimensions each position may emit. We further apply a simple vocabulary merging strategy that removes redundant entries - such as case and word-boundary variants of the same word - which are common in cased BPE-based backbones.
We apply our recipe to the LateOn backbone and training data, obtaining SPARSEUP, a sparse encoder that reaches 56.4 average nDCG@10 on BEIR-13, the highest we know of among public vocabulary-based sparse encoders below 150M parameters.
papers.summary: Sparse retrievers like SPLADE, moved onto newer backbones such as ModernBERT, often train poorly, and RoBERTa does not train at all. The authors trace this to the starting point: most of the new backbones' vocabulary scores are already positive, so at the start of training almost every term is active, the document representation is dense, and the gradient that tells terms apart weakens. The fix has three steps. Before training, one constant is subtracted from all scores, set at a high percentile of the score distribution estimated on a small sample of documents. Each input position may activate at most 12 terms. Case and word-boundary variants of the same word are merged. The final model reaches 56.4 average nDCG@10 on BEIR, only 1.5 points below a dense model trained on the same backbone and data. Anyone moving sparse retrieval to a new backbone can start with these three steps.

papers.title: FondueQA: A Benchmark for Evaluating Parametric Compensation in Multi-Hop QA
papers.authors: Laurin Schmid, Suman Navaratnarajah, Koel Dutta Chowdhury, Steffen Eger, Josif Grabocka, Christian Frey
papers.abstract:
Large Language Models (LLMs) show remarkable performance based on parametric knowledge, i.e., their ability to recall facts and associations internalized in a model's weights. However, studying this capability on established multi-hop benchmarks may be complicated by benchmark contamination, as many of these benchmarks have been publicly available long enough to plausibly appear in modern pretraining corpora.
As a result, correct answers under missing evidence may reflect either general parametric knowledge or memorization of benchmark-specific instances. To study how models use internal knowledge when retrieval evidence is incomplete, we introduce FondueQA, in which every required multi-hop fact is uniquely localized to a designated evidence document. This enables controlled document-level evidence ablations to study parametric compensation under incomplete retrieval.
Our empirical evaluation reveals that parametric compensation strongly depends on both entity popularity and the structural role of missing evidence. Generally, models compensate more successfully for facts involving popular entities. On FondueQA, we show that bridging evidence can be more useful than the answer-bearing document itself.
Moreover, models may recall a missing fact in isolation but fail to use it under partial evidence, particularly when the context contains plausible competing entities, which can reduce Exact Match by up to 15 percentage points.
papers.summary: Ask "What is the nationality of the director of Titanic?" If retrieval can return only one document, which one helps more? Intuition says the one holding the answer, the document stating that director James Cameron is Canadian. The authors find that keeping the bridge document, the one stating that Cameron directed the film, often works better, especially for smaller models: once the model knows whom to look up, it can often fill in the missing fact from its own memory. To run such comparisons, they built a multi-hop QA set, FondueQA, where each needed fact appears in exactly one designated document, so documents can be removed one at a time. The more popular the entity behind a missing fact, the more easily models fill it in. But adding a few plausible competing entities to the context can cut some models' accuracy by about 15 percentage points. In RAG, besides how much is retrieved, it matters which link of the reasoning chain is kept.

papers.title: MARS: Training Multilingual Search Agents for Retriever-Free Evidence Acquisition
papers.authors: Rui Qi, Yunlong Liang, Yufeng Chen, Jinan Xu, Fandong Meng, Kaiyu Huang
papers.abstract: Existing multilingual retrieval-augmented generation relies heavily on learned retrievers and similarity-based ranking from multilingual collections, which are vulnerable to cross-lingual retrieval errors and indexing overhead. In this paper, we explore retriever-free multilingual search, where the model directly interacts with raw corpora through executable shell commands. This paradigm shifts the bottleneck to multilingual search action generation, where exact search is sensitive to entity surface forms and outcome-only supervision provides limited guidance for multi-turn search. To address these challenges, we propose MARS, a multilingual search agent in direct corpus interaction (DCI) with reinforcement learning (RL). MARS introduces corpus-native entity grounding to recover reliable lexical anchors from corpus evidence, mitigating failure to retrieve evidence. Meanwhile, we present a redundancy-aware search reward to encourage concise and effective search trajectories, addressing
papers.summary: Multilingual retrieval-augmented generation usually builds an index first and then ranks with a trained retriever, and a slight change in how an entity is spelled across languages can send the search to the wrong place. This work lets the model issue executable search commands against the raw corpus and trains it with reinforcement learning. It first searches the corpus to verify each entity's native spelling, then reuses those spellings in later queries. Each search command is treated as a set of terms. If the intersection-over-union of two sets exceeds a chosen threshold, the commands are treated as near-duplicates and merged. only a trajectory that finally answers correctly receives a reward scaled by the fraction of commands that remain distinct. On MKQA and MLQA, average accuracy rises 3.2 points over GrepSeek and replies become 29% shorter. Repeated searches fall while cross-lingual generalization still holds.

papers.title: EAGR: Evidence-Guided Adaptive Graph Retrieval
papers.authors: Sonam Gupta, Vignesh P, Vishwajeet Kumar, Adnan Qidwai, Anand Eswaran, Jaydeep Sen, Sachindra Joshi
papers.abstract:
Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) for multi-hop reasoning requires retrieval to adapt as intermediate evidence reveals new information needs. Existing approaches support such retrieval through explicit graph structures or iterative query reformulation, introducing graph-construction or query-time overhead.
We present Evidence-Guided Adaptive Graph Retrieval (EAGR), a framework in which accumulated evidence dynamically determines which semantic directions to explore next, and which requires no dedicated graph database and no explicit graph materialization. EAGR operates over an implicit semantic graph induced by compact passage metadata pre-ingested into a standard VectorDB.
Starting from dense-retrieval seed passages, an LLM iteratively assesses accumulated evidence, identifies promising semantic directions, expands the retrieval frontier through metadata-based neighborhood lookup, and terminates once sufficient evidence has been collected. By precomputing semantic metadata, EAGR enables evidence-conditioned graph exploration without materializing an explicit graph, maintaining a dedicated GraphDB, or iteratively rewriting the query.
Across three widely used multi-hop QA benchmarks, EAGR achieves the highest LLM-based answer accuracy among evaluated methods, outperforming the vanilla RAG by 17\% and strongest graph-aware baseline by 4\% percentage points averaged across three popular benchmarks HotPotQA, 2WikiMultiHopQA, and MuSiQue.
papers.summary: Ask who someone's mother-in-law is, and a first retrieval rarely finds the answer: you first need the passage about their spouse, then follow the spouse to her mother. Where to search next only becomes clear once intermediate evidence arrives. Common approaches either build a knowledge graph in advance or have an LLM rewrite the query at every step. The first needs a separate store to build and maintain, the second adds a round of work per step. At ingestion, EAGR has an LLM extract descriptors such as entities from each passage and stores them as ordinary metadata in the vector database, so passages sharing a descriptor count as neighbors. At query time, dense retrieval finds a few starting passages. The LLM reads the evidence so far, picks the descriptors worth following, fetches neighboring passages through the metadata, and stops once the evidence suffices. Averaged over three multi-hop QA datasets, LLM-judged accuracy is 67.1%, against 59.8% for vanilla RAG and 63.2% for the strongest graph-based baseline.

papers.title: Orthogonal Norm Growth in Two-Tower Retrieval: A Popularity Mechanism for Unified Discovery
papers.abstract: Unified search and recommendation systems may update the same item vectors from both interaction streams. We study how repeated updates can increase an item vector's norm and affect retrieval under an unnormalized dot product. A cosine-only loss makes the output gradient perpendicular to the current item vector - tangent to its constant-norm sphere. Training changes encoder parameters, however, so the realized item-vector movement need not remain tangent. We derive sufficient conditions under which it does; every nonzero update then increases squared norm by its squared length. When the tasks share an item encoder, sequential updates from both can accumulate in the same norm, which raw-inner-product serving can expose for either task. This conditional result is not a theorem about joint SGD. Controlled ablations test these conditions. On MovieLens 32M and Amazon Books, accumulated tangent movement accompanies frequency-norm association and additional head-item exposure under raw-dot ra
papers.summary: When search and recommendation share the same item vectors, their updates can jointly push some vectors to grow longer. In unnormalized dot-product retrieval, items with larger norms are easier to retrieve. The authors prove that, under stated sufficiency conditions, a cosine-loss gradient moves tangent to the equal-norm sphere, so each nonzero update increases the squared norm by the squared length of that tangential step. Training also updates encoder parameters, so the actual move need not stay tangent. On MovieLens 32M and Amazon Books, this tangent accumulation comes with a correlation between frequency and norm. Ranking with the raw unnormalized dot product retrieves more head items than first normalizing the item vectors. A control that, after each item-id vector update, retracts the immediate norm change from that step weakens this exposure, but recommendation quality also drops, so the control is a diagnosis rather than a fix the authors recommend.

papers.title: Whispers from the Neighbors: Rethinking Caption Consensus as Inference-Time Evidence for Vision-Language Retrieval
papers.authors: Khang Nhat Hoang Vo, Belal Shoer, Abhirama Subramanyam Penamakuri
papers.abstract: An image is rarely described only once. Retrieval benchmarks and many collections attach several captions to each picture, yet dual encoders still judge every image-caption pair in isolation. We ask what these neighboring captions contribute when a frozen encoder consults them at inference time. Fusing image similarity with similarity to an image's own captions improves text-to-image R@1 by 3.4 to 16.8 points across nine frozen encoders when the captions come from the same annotators as the queries. The gain falls to 1.9 to 7.2 points when an off-the-shelf captioner writes them, and to at most one point when they come from a different annotation source; a paraphrase-trained text encoder strengthens the text side further. A natural refinement, scoring the part of the image that the captions leave unexplained, appears to add much more under a leave-one-out evaluation. We show that this advantage arises because the correct candidate's supports are built differently from those of the negat
papers.summary: An image is rarely described only once: retrieval benchmarks often attach several captions to the same picture, yet dual-encoder models still score each image-text pair on its own. This paper asks how much a frozen encoder gains at inference if it also looks at the other captions of the same image. It averages and normalizes those caption vectors into a consensus, then adds a weighted combination of the consensus-to-query text similarity and the image-to-query similarity. When the captions and the queries come from the same annotators, text-to-image R@1 rises by 3.4 to 16.8 points across nine frozen encoders. If an off-the-shelf captioner writes the captions instead, the gain shrinks to 1.9 to 7.2 points. The captions help match a candidate to how people describe the image, rather than improving image-text alignment itself.

papers.title: Differentially Private GraphRAG: Protecting Relation Connectivity and Semantics
papers.authors: Jie Fu, Yuan Hong, Yue Ning, Wendy Hui Wang
papers.abstract: Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation (GraphRAG) connects information across documents through entity relationships to support relational reasoning. However, black-box access to GraphRAG systems can enable adversaries to reconstruct knowledge graphs and recover both structural connectivity between entities and the semantics of their relationships. Existing defenses lack formal privacy guarantees and provide limited protection against such reconstruction attacks. We propose RelGuard, the first differentially private framework for GraphRAG, which provides formal privacy guarantees by mitigating connectivity leakage and protecting relations and their semantic meaning through relation removal. We formalize relation differential privacy (relation-DP), which bounds the distinguishability of mechanism outputs according to the semantic distance between alternative relations while accounting for relation removal. Building on this definition, we develop a four-step defense mechanism that sanitize
papers.summary: Graph retrieval-augmented generation links entity relations in documents into a knowledge graph so a model can reason over those links. With only black-box access, an attacker may still reconstruct the graph, recovering both whether two entities are connected and what the edge means. Before indexing, this work extracts triples, generates candidate predicates, and uses the exponential mechanism to sample a replacement phrasing or a null outcome. Utility is the negative semantic distance between a candidate phrasing and the original relation, so closer meanings are more likely to be drawn; a null draw deletes the edge and has a fixed utility that does not depend on the original wording. Across three graph-RAG systems and two targeted reconstruction attacks, relation-recovery F1 falls 26.98% to 44.35% versus the strongest baseline. Question-answering F1 drops only 2.98% to 8.97%.

papers.title: Less Is More: Graph-free Multimodal RAG via Multi-signal Late Fusion
papers.authors: Tithi Rakshit, Hongkuan Zhou, Lavdim Halilaj, Yuqicheng Zhu
papers.abstract:
Graph-based retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) is widely used for multimodal, cross-document question answering. However, building corpus-level graphs is expensive, slow to query, and difficult to maintain. We present TrioRAG, a graph-free multimodal framework that integrates evidence from three complementary signals: the question, the anchor image, and a VLM-enhanced query generated from both.
Each signal retrieves independently over a shared multi-vector index of page text and page images, and the results are combined through late fusion. Further, we introduce AutoQA, a multimodal automotive benchmark whose questions are grounded in noisy, web-sourced images rather than clean document-sourced figures. Its questions require reasoning across manuals. We position it as a model-curated testbed rather than a human-validated gold standard.
Across three benchmarks, TrioRAG matches or outperforms graph-based systems while reducing total cost and accelerating per-query inference by 1.6-2.3 times. By construction, AutoQA grounds its questions in out-of-corpus web images. In this setting image retrieval reaches only 19.3% document-level recall, while text-derived signals, especially the VLM-enhanced query, keep retrieval robust.
papers.summary: For multimodal cross-document QA, many systems first extract entities from the whole corpus and build a joint text-image knowledge graph, then retrieve over the graph. Building the graph is expensive and slow, and any document change means extracting again. TrioRAG builds no graph. It puts each page's text and page image into one multi-vector index and retrieves with three signals: the question text, the image attached to the question, and a question rewritten by a vision-language model that looks at the image. The three rankings are then merged. On three benchmarks it matches or beats two graph-based systems, and its total time including indexing is 12 to 65 times shorter. The authors also built AutoQA, an automotive QA set whose images come from the web and are not in the corpus. There, image retrieval alone reaches only 19.3% document recall, and the two text signals carry retrieval. For multimodal RAG over frequently updated documents, this graph-free setup is worth trying first.

papers.title: Improving Contextual Retrieval for Long Documents using Semantic Chunking and Hybrid Retrieval Strategies
papers.abstract: The vast amount of information available in lengthy, distributed documents makes finding relevant answers difficult, especially when the answer requires connecting evidence from multiple sources. Standard Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) systems often struggle with this type of "multi-hop" reasoning and frequently face issues with context fragmentation. In this paper, we propose a hybrid RAG framework that integrates the structured reasoning of knowledge graphs with the broad semantic coverage of dense vector retrieval. Our approach employs a multi-stage pipeline using transformer-based summarization and semantic chunking to improve context retention. We construct a dynamic knowledge graph to capture explicit relationships between entities while simultaneously maintaining a dense vector index. During inference, the system uses a hierarchical mechanism that prioritizes graph traversal for precision and falls back to vector retrieval when necessary. We evaluated our framework on the
papers.summary: When an answer has to join evidence spread across long documents, ordinary retrieval-augmented generation tends to fragment the context and struggles with multi-hop reasoning. This work keeps both the explicit relations in a knowledge graph and the semantic coverage of dense vector retrieval. At inference it ranks entities by how densely they are connected and starts graph traversal from the most informative ones, following paths that link those entities. Each path is scored from the semantic similarity between its edge labels and the query terms, how often that relation appears across document segments, and a penalty on overly long or looping chains. Only if no path is found, or this combined score is too low, does it fall back to encoding the query as a vector and retrieving with dense search plus keyword matching. On MultiHop-RAG, the hybrid method reaches 55.8% exact match, compared with 51.5% for vector retrieval alone and 48.7% for the graph alone.

papers.title: SkinMind: Equipping Agentic RAG with Human-Inspired Graph Probing for Reliable Dermatology AI
papers.authors: Jing Hao, Weinan Zhou, Zhihong Lu, Yaling Shen, Yiming Xu, Yefeng Liu, Siyuan Yan, Shuaibo Li, Ming Dai, Junjun He, Zuyi Zhu, Jinjie Gu, Lijun Wu, Jian Wang
papers.abstract:
Reliable dermatology AI requires access to verifiable evidence distributed across heterogeneous textual and visual sources. However, conventional retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) typically relies on one-shot retrieval from flat corpora, limiting its ability to adapt retrieval granularity, explore multi-hop relations, and integrate multimodal clinical evidence.
We introduce SkinMind, a multimodal agentic RAG framework that equips policy models with human-inspired graph probing for autonomous evidence seeking. SkinMind organizes retrieval as an iterative interaction between an orchestrator and a graph environment. Through eight hierarchical graph-probing tools, the orchestrator progressively identifies relevant entities, inspects node-level information, traverses relations and paths, and retrieves source-text and visual evidence.
This progressive-disclosure design allows the model to adaptively determine the retrieval modality, exploration direction, and evidence granularity while constructing a query-specific evidence subgraph. To support autonomous graph probing, we construct SkinMind-KG from a 62M-token corpus of dermatology guidelines and textbooks and 423K images, guided by a dermatologist-informed schema and a conflict-resolution mechanism.
The resulting graph contains over 1.0M nodes and 2.0M edges, unifying textual, relational, and visual evidence for retrieval. Across six dermatology VQA benchmarks and two policy-model settings, SkinMind improves the average score over direct answering by 8.70 and 8.89 points with GPT-5.4-mini and Gemini-2.5-Flash, respectively, while consistently outperforming competing RAG methods.
Together, SkinMind and SkinMind-KG provide an effective foundation for evidence-grounded multimodal reasoning in dermatology.
papers.summary: Dermatology questions often need guideline text, relations between diseases, and lesion images at the same time, and a single retrieval pass over a text corpus rarely gathers all of that. SkinMind first builds a joint text-image knowledge graph from dermatology guidelines and textbooks, with over a million nodes, then treats it as an environment to probe step by step. The orchestrating LLM has eight tools. It can find relevant entities, inspect node details, follow relations and paths, and finally pull source passages and images as evidence. What to query at each step, and at what granularity, depends on the clues gathered so far. The authors average scores over six dermatology visual QA benchmarks: accuracy on five multiple-choice sets, and an LLM judge comparing answers with references on one open-ended set. With one orchestrator model, the average rises from 59.20 with direct answering to 67.90. The other orchestrator model gains about as much, and SkinMind consistently beats other RAG methods. The graph is opened up as tools for step-by-step probing rather than used only as a retrieval index.

papers.title: Structure and Lineage Evidence for Vietnamese Statutory Article Retrieval on DRiLL
papers.abstract:
We study Vietnamese statutory Article retrieval on DRiLL using features for provision identity and local form, same-law support, and citation and lineage evidence. Across five random seeds, selectors sharing candidates, listwise Qwen evidence, and learner settings improve official $F_2$ from 71.77% to 72.91%, with the largest descriptive gain on two-Article questions.
Added features account for 18.20% of the proposed selector's total decision-tree split gain, measured as training-objective reduction, mainly from same-law and citation evidence. Cases reveal base provisions and amendments, companion recovery, distractor removal, and failures. These findings motivate research on other datasets, representations, and learners without establishing individual feature effects or requiring LightGBM, hand-crafted scores, or explicit graphs.
papers.summary: In Vietnamese legal QA, answering one question often means finding several statutory Articles together, such as a base provision and a later Article that amends it. Retrieval by wording similarity alone easily misses amendments and companion Articles. On DRiLL, a Vietnamese statutory Article retrieval dataset, the authors add several kinds of structural features to each candidate Article: which law it belongs to, which other candidates come from the same law, what it cites, and what has amended it. LightGBM then combines these with LLM relevance judgments to pick the final answer. Averaged over five random seeds, the official F2 score rises from 71.77% to 72.91%, a small gain that is clearest on questions needing two Articles. Among the added features, same-law and citation evidence contribute most. For anyone who wants to use citation and amendment links in legal retrieval, the paper offers a concrete feature list.

papers.title: A Taxonomy-Driven Synthetic Dataset for Retrieval Effectiveness and Fairness Evaluation in Hiring
papers.authors: Warren Jouanneau, Morgane Hoffmann, Emma Jouffroy, Marc Palyart
papers.abstract:
While machine learning hiring tools are ubiquitous, the need for privacy regulations and commercial sensitivity makes public benchmarking legally complex. We address this challenge by introducing a taxonomy-driven, fully synthetic HR dataset and benchmark to simultaneously evaluate retrieval effectiveness and algorithmic fairness. Grounded in 660K real freelancer profiles, our multilingual corpus features candidate profiles, project briefs, and counterfactual demographic twins.
Auditing state-of-the-art embedding models reveals performance divergence from general MTEB scores, alongside fairness disparities in grammatically gendered languages. This demonstrates that general benchmarks are insufficient for HR, requiring tailored evaluations to identify Pareto-optimal models that balance semantic accuracy and fairness.
papers.summary: Retrieval models for hiring are hard to benchmark publicly, because real resumes and job requirements involve privacy and commercial secrets. Starting from a large set of real freelancer profiles and a taxonomy of occupations and skills, the authors use Gemini to synthesize multilingual candidate profiles and project briefs. Each profile gets a counterfactual twin that is identical except that gendered word forms are switched between masculine and feminine. Testing embedding models on it shows that general MTEB rankings do not carry over well: Arctic Embed scores lower on the general multilingual board, yet its NDCG@10 on project-brief retrieval is 0.07 higher than several instruction-tuned models. Model size also shows no systematic link to fairness, and models of similar size can react very differently to the gender switch. When choosing a model for hiring search, test effectiveness and fairness together in your own setting.
